extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, forensic investigators, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for using induction, analogy, and probability in criminal investigation and proof; explains when single instances suffice, how to treat negative assertions, the danger and limited role of analogy, and the proper use of probability versus proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish empirical laws cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical rule is no final law but is capable of explaining observed regularities; empirical laws must be established by systematic study and inductive procedure before being treated as generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws may explain succession of conditions (e.g., weather signs, species improvement, hardness of alloys) but should not be assumed to be 'natural law' until subjected to inductive procedure. Criminalistics has produced few such internally derived laws and requires systematic reduction and study of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limits of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the reference of facts discovered by experience to general laws or the generalization/universalization of our experiences; it infers that a phenomenon occurring x times will occur again when essential circumstances remain identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific induction requires certainty and accuracy in addition to observation and deduction. Beware that many criminal-generalizations rest only on limited experience and thus lack the certainty of well-established scientific inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use great caution when generalizing from limited experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminalists' experience is limited in scope and duration, so extending inductions from familiar to markedly different cases (e.g., educated persons to peasants) requires great caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously remind oneself of the scantiness of material and avoid uncritical transfer of patterns observed in a narrow sample to fundamentally different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction and analogy share foundations; both can mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is intimately related to analogy; both rest on the same foundation and can be unjustified when one takes something as 'sufficient' that is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many common doctrines (value of witnesses, confessions, composition of testimony) depend on induction and analogy; because of their pervasiveness they must either be reliable or handled with greatest care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish positive versus negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive statements may be justified by a single instance; negative assertions require complete enumeration of all possible instances and are often boundless and not fully answerable by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase questions to match intent: asking 'Are there any white marbles?' is a positive question answered by one example; asking 'Are there only white marbles?' is effectively negative and requires exhaustive proof. Treat negative claims with recognition of their practical unanswerability in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse the thing proved with the point at issue (positive evidence limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing agreement of particular relations (e.g., shoe length, width, number of nails) proves those relations but does not necessarily prove the identity of the actor; such positive matches calculate probability rather than establish absolute proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on matching particulars (footprint to shoe), explicitly assess the probability that another person could share those particulars; recognize that positive evidence frequently only yields probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative portion of evidence requires equal accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative evidence (showing absence of alternatives) is often developed with less accuracy and yet is essential; neglecting it leaves the proof probabilistic rather than conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine and attempt to falsify alternative hypotheses (e.g., prevalence of a shoe type in the region) rather than only showing a positive fit; avoid treating the positive portion as sufficient when negative possibilities exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert 'not' statements are often deduced positive identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative expert statement (e.g., 'this is not blood') usually rests on a positive identification of something else (e.g., rust stain), so 'negation' may in practice be a positive empirical judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand the underlying positive basis for any categorical negation from experts; understand the inference chain rather than taking bare 'not' claims at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical connection from experiential grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inferences depend primarily on logical relationships, others on empirical associations; both have experiential premises, but one foregrounds formal logic while the other foregrounds experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing conclusions, test whether the chain of reasoning is formal/logical or empirical, and check that the empirical premises are correct—logical correctness cannot save a false premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overconfidence in logical work without empirical verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive and careful logical work can be rendered worthless if based on an unexamined or false empirical presupposition; there is a tendency to neglect empirical checks after heavy logical effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always review the empirical premises behind logical deductions; be aware of the subconscious tendency to 'compensate' heavy work in one area with neglect in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy requires demonstrable relation between the compared attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy rests on the postulate that items sharing many qualities will agree in additional qualities; its value depends on whether a genuine relation exists between the compared attributes (e.g., clouds→rain is meaningful; color→perfume is not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate analogies by asking whether a common causal or explanatory basis supports the inferred additional quality; without such a basis the analogy is worthless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy is dangerous and overused in unfamiliar or emotive cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with strange or troubling facts, jurors and lawyers tend to impose analogies drawn from their own experience or profession, often inappropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against analogical reasoning that imports irrelevant professional or personal schemas; require justification for analogies rather than allowing intuitive parallels to drive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analogy to constructions/hypotheses and test them
rubrics_metrics.description: The only appropriate use of analogy in investigative work is for making 'constructions'—assumptions that render an unintelligible case intelligible and can be progressively tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogy to propose hypotheses, but treat them as provisional tools: test them against material, eliminate inconsistencies, and do not elevate successful constructions to proved facts without independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the variable certainty of analogy (analogy vs law)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the postulate underlying an analogy is highly certain, the relation is a law rather than an analogy; if the postulate is uncertain, analogy gives little, possibly deceptive, guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish when you are positing a conjectural analogy versus when you are invoking an established causal law; this determines the weight you may properly give the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate assumption, probability, and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: What one desires leads to assumption, what is possible gives probability, and what appears certain is called proved; probability is a lower degree of certainty and has a primarily heuristic role for criminalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize assumptions as necessary starting points (heuristic/hypotheses) and that even high probability alone is not proof for purposes like sentencing; treat probability as corroborative unless aggregated evidence produces certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: High probability is corroborative but not equivalent to proof; sentencing requires certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A very high degree of probability can justify complaints or investigative steps, but sentencing requires 'certainty'—probability may only serve corroborative weight unless many independent high probabilities coincide to render certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate independent probable indices (e.g., recognition, failed alibi, footprints, possession of stolen goods) can sometimes produce effective certainty; nevertheless, do not equate single high-probability indicators with proof for conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability has a heuristic investigative role
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions and probabilities are valuable heuristics for guiding inquiry and forming hypotheses in difficult or partially known cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assumptions to begin inquiry; abandon or replace them when inconsistent and iterate until a workable probable hypothesis emerges that can be further tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conditioned versus unconditioned probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditioned probability is based on current, specific conditions (e.g., facts known about the case); unconditioned probability is drawn from statistical history or overall frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting unconditioned (statistical) probabilities for conditioned assessments tied to the particular facts at hand; compute conditioned probabilities when possible for case-specific evaluation (example: assessing likelihood of discovery given current facts vs using general murder-discovery rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about probability's formulation and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability may be conceived mathematically (fraction of favorable cases among equally possible cases), epistemically (dependence on knowledge/ignorance), or as an objective tendency; its interpretation affects how it should be used in reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether you are using probability as mathematical conditioned estimation, as a heuristic based on ignorance/knowledge (Laplace), or as an objective measure (Venn), since confusion among these conceptions can lead to erroneous inferences in criminal cases.
